title: SHE POURED EXPENSIVE PERFUME ON JESUS — EVERYONE SAW WASTE, BUT JESUS SAW WORSHIP
paragraphs: SHE POURED EXPENSIVE PERFUME ON JESUS — EVERYONE SAW WASTE, BUT JESUS SAW WORSHIP

They calculated what her worship cost. Jesus saw what her heart was worth. And before you finish this story, you may discover there is an alabaster jar in your own hands that you have been afraid to break.
There are moments in Scripture that do not merely ask to be read.
They ask you to enter the room.
Come close enough to hear the voices around the table. Close enough to notice the tension gathering around Jesus. Close enough to smell the perfume when it suddenly fills the room.
Because somewhere in this story, you may recognize yourself.
And maybe that is why this story still refuses to die.
Jesus is only days away from the cross.

Mark places this extraordinary scene in the shadow of betrayal. Religious leaders are already looking for a way to arrest and kill Him. Immediately after the woman’s act of devotion, Judas goes to betray Him.
Jesus is reclining at a meal in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, when a woman walks into the room carrying something extraordinarily valuable.
Mark describes it in Greek as:
An alabaster vessel containing costly perfume of nard.
Something that could be converted into money.

Mark tells us the perfume was valued at more than three hundred denarii. A denarius was commonly associated with a laborer’s daily wage, which helps explain the staggering value involved. This was not the ancient equivalent of spraying a little fragrance into the air. This represented an enormous economic sacrifice.
And then she does something that makes the room uncomfortable.
She does not merely loosen a lid and carefully measure out a respectable amount.
Then she pours the perfume upon Jesus.
There is something breathtaking about worship that has stopped negotiating.
No whispered question of, “How little can I give and still call this devotion?”
And suddenly the fragrance is everywhere.
While she is worshiping, somebody else is doing the math.
And this is where the story becomes painfully modern.
Give too much to Jesus, and someone will call you extreme.
Forgive somebody who does not deserve it, and someone will call you weak.
Walk away from a profitable compromise because Christ matters more, and someone will call you foolish.
Choose purity when everyone around you has normalized sin, and someone will call you old-fashioned.
Spend your time serving people who can never repay you, and someone will ask what you are getting out of it.
Talk too passionately about Jesus, and somebody will quietly decide that you have become “too religious.”
There will always be people who can calculate the cost of your obedience while remaining incapable of understanding its value.
The people in that room looked at the perfume and saw money disappearing.
Jesus looked at the woman and saw worship.
Their question, preserved in Greek, was devastating:
Εἰς τί ἡ ἀπώλεια αὕτη τοῦ μύρου γέγονεν;
Eis ti hē apōleia hautē tou myrou gegonen?
Why has this waste of the perfume happened?
They looked at something poured upon Jesus and called it waste.
And perhaps you know what that feels like.
You finally started following Christ seriously, and somebody mocked you.
You surrendered a relationship you knew was pulling you away from God, and somebody told you that you were throwing away happiness.
And someone looked at the life you were laying before Jesus and wondered why you were wasting it.
But there is a question beneath this passage that cannot be avoided:
Can anything truly surrendered to Jesus be called wasted?
And then Christ speaks words she desperately needed to hear:
Everyone else is discussing your failure to meet their expectations.
Everyone else has reduced your devotion to numbers.
There are people reading this who have lived for years under voices Jesus never assigned to govern them.
The voice of the person who humiliated you.
The parent who made you believe you would never be enough.
The church person who knew Scripture but used it like a weapon.
The former partner whose rejection became the mirror through which you began seeing yourself.
The friend who disappeared when your life became inconvenient.
The voice inside your own head repeating every failure after God has called you to repentance and faith.
Somewhere along the way, human condemnation became louder than divine mercy.
Jesus does not call evil good. Grace never means pretending sin does not matter. The same Christ who receives sinners calls sinners to repentance.
The Gospel is not Jesus helping us become comfortable with darkness.
The Gospel is Jesus rescuing us from it.
Yet the person who comes to Christ does not come to a Savior standing at a distance with folded arms.
We come to the Lamb who went to the cross.
We come unable to purchase our cleansing.
And Christ offers what money, morality, reputation, religion, and self-improvement could never buy.
That is why Christianity is not fundamentally the story of good people becoming slightly better.
It is the story of sinners being reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
And this woman’s perfume is poured beneath the growing shadow of that cross.
Jesus explains her act with words even she may not have fully understood:
προέλαβεν μυρίσαι τὸ σῶμά μου εἰς τὸν ἐνταφιασμόν
She has anointed His body beforehand for burial.
This is no longer merely perfume.
The fragrance is pointing toward a tomb.
Jesus knows where He is going.
The disciples repeatedly struggle to understand.
The woman pours out something precious upon Jesus...
while Jesus is preparing to pour Himself out for sinners.
That is the part we cannot miss.
This is where Christian worship begins.
Not with what we give Jesus.
With what Jesus has done for us.
We love because He first loved us.
We surrender because the King first came to save sinners who could never save themselves.
We do not purchase grace with sacrifice.
We sacrifice because grace has already confronted us with the immeasurable worth of Christ.
You cannot buy God's love by giving enough money.
You cannot earn forgiveness by sharing a Christian article.
You cannot secure heaven by buying a Christian book, wearing a Christian shirt, or donating to Christian work.
Salvation is God's gift received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Our support, generosity, service, sharing, and sacrifice are responses to grace—not the price of grace.
And once grace truly grips the heart, something changes.
“Jesus, after everything You have done for me, what am I still refusing to surrender?”
Because perhaps your alabaster jar is not money.
Your relationship that you know is leading you away from Christ.
Your bitterness toward somebody who wounded you years ago.
The apology you refuse to make.
The person you refuse to forgive.
The part of your future you want Jesus to bless but refuse to let Him govern.
We often tell Jesus, “You can have everything.”
And somehow the jar remains unbroken.
That is why this woman is uncomfortable.
She walked into a room full of opinions and decided Jesus was worth more than all of them.
And Mark gives us one of the most beautiful sentences Christ ever spoke about an act of discipleship:
Not what she wished she could.
Not what would impress the room.
There are believers torturing themselves because they cannot do what somebody else does.
And perhaps Jesus is not asking you for somebody else's alabaster jar.
He is asking what is in your hands.
Maybe your worship today is getting out of bed and praying when depression has made everything feel heavy.
Maybe it is deleting the number.
Asking forgiveness from the person you hurt.
Choosing truth when lying would protect your image.
Turning away from pornography when nobody would know.
Coming back to church after disappointment.
Whispering, “Jesus, help me,” because those are the only words your exhausted heart can produce.
Never confuse hidden obedience with insignificant obedience.
But there is another person hovering around this story.

John's Gospel identifies the woman at the Bethany anointing as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus, and tells us that she anointed Jesus' feet and wiped them with her hair. John also tells us something Mark leaves more general: Judas Iscariot objected to the expense, speaking as though his concern were for the poor, while John exposes his corrupt motive. The Gospel accounts emphasize different details without changing the central reality: costly perfume was poured upon Jesus in Bethany, criticism followed, and Jesus defended the act.
That contrast should frighten anyone who has learned how to sound spiritual.
Because it is possible to use righteous vocabulary while protecting an unrighteous heart.
But Jesus knew what was underneath both.
That should make every one of us examine ourselves.
Sometimes jealousy disguises itself as discernment.
Sometimes we criticize another person's devotion because their surrender exposes our own compromise.
Sometimes “wisdom” is simply the respectable name we have given our unwillingness to obey.
And sometimes we become so experienced at Christianity that we can stand near Jesus without being moved by Jesus.
And still his heart could be somewhere else.
Physical proximity to Christian things is not the same as surrender to Christ.
You can know worship songs and not worship.
You can post Bible verses and remain unrepentant.
You can attend church and hide secret sin.
You can defend Christian doctrine online while being cruel to your family offline.
You can call Jesus “Lord” publicly while continually telling Him “no” privately.
But scandal is not where the Gospel ends.
Grace always costs more than the sinner understands because the cost ultimately falls upon Christ.
Soon Jesus would be treated as though He were disposable.
The world would look upon the suffering Messiah and see weakness.
What appeared to be defeat would become victory.
What looked like the end would become the beginning.
The grave would not keep Him.
And that changes the meaning of every surrendered life.
Your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
Your shame does not have to become your identity.
Your past does not possess authority greater than the blood of Christ.
But grace is not permission to keep clutching the very chains Jesus died to break.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace brings the sinner to the cross empty-handed and sends the redeemed person away with a new Master.
Perhaps that is why you are still reading.
Maybe this stopped being a story about perfume several paragraphs ago.
Maybe God has placed His finger on something.
Something you have protected because breaking it feels too expensive.
And maybe the question is no longer whether Jesus is worthy.
Maybe the question is whether you actually believe He is.
The woman broke the jar because worship had become more valuable than preservation.
She could not pour it out and still keep it.
There comes a point when surrender has to become more than vocabulary.
Because we have encountered the Savior.
Jesus then says something astonishing about her:
Wherever the Gospel is proclaimed throughout the world, what she did would be told in memory of her.
Think about where you are right now.
Think about the centuries between her room and yours.
Her alabaster vessel shattered and vanished into history.
Jesus called it worthy of remembrance.
Never let a temporary audience define the eternal value of obedience.
And now this story has reached your hands.
So what will you do with it?
Let the comments become more than engagement.
A reminder to the person scrolling beneath you that they are not the only one fighting to keep their eyes on Jesus.
Sharing cannot earn God's favor, but it can place biblical truth in front of someone who might never have searched for it themselves.
Not because supporting us earns favor with God.
And never because salvation can be bought.
But before you leave, return once more to Bethany.
And Jesus is watching the woman everyone else has decided to judge.
They smell expensive perfume disappearing into the air.
Jesus smells the fragrance of surrender.
And perhaps somewhere in your life right now there is still an alabaster jar sitting safely in your hands.
But the woman of Bethany leaves us with a question that follows us long after the fragrance disappears:
If Jesus truly gave Himself for you, what are you still afraid to pour out for Him?
This may have hit harder than you expected.
The perfume can be poured out.
Your carefully constructed life can fall apart.
But when everything you thought defined you lies shattered at the feet of Jesus, you may finally discover that the safest place for a broken life was at His feet all along.
